Every statute in this wiki rests on a handful of clauses in Articles I and II. Congress holds the war, money, and military-rulemaking powers; the President is commander in chief and conducts diplomacy. The founding-era statutes show Congress using those powers early: calling out the militia, policing private war-making, and controlling enemy aliens. Start here, then learn how the U.S. Code files the laws that followed.

## What you should be able to do

- Name the constitutional clauses that divide war and foreign affairs powers.
- Explain why formal declarations of war stopped after 1942.
- Distinguish an enacted statute from its place in the U.S. Code.

### Court cases

::: {.reading-card .case-card .domain-foundations}
[Curtiss-Wright](../../cases/curtiss-wright-1936.qmd) [299 U.S. 304 (1936)]{.reading-year} [Court case]{.layer-badge}

Upheld the delegation. Because foreign affairs powers rest on national sovereignty rather than on the Constitution's specific grants alone, Congress may give the President broader discretion abroad than at home.

[Read it: [opinion](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-299/pdf/USREPORTS-299-304.pdf)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="curtiss-wright-1936"> I have read this</label>
:::

::: {.reading-card .case-card .domain-foundations}
[Youngstown](../../cases/youngstown-1952.qmd) [343 U.S. 579 (1952)]{.reading-year} [Court case]{.layer-badge}

Held the seizure unlawful. No statute authorized it, and the President's powers as Commander in Chief and chief executive did not extend to taking private property at home to settle a labor dispute; that was lawmaking reserved to Congress.

[Read it: [opinion](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-343/pdf/USREPORTS-343-579.pdf)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="youngstown-1952"> I have read this</label>
:::

::: {.reading-card .case-card .domain-foundations}
[INS v. Chadha](../../cases/chadha-1983.qmd) [462 U.S. 919 (1983)]{.reading-year} [Court case]{.layer-badge}

No. Action with the effect of law must pass both houses and be presented to the President.

[Read it: [opinion](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-462/pdf/USREPORTS-462-919.pdf)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="chadha-1983"> I have read this</label>
:::

::: {.reading-card .case-card .domain-foundations}
[Zivotofsky v. Kerry](../../cases/zivotofsky-2015.qmd) [576 U.S. 1 (2015)]{.reading-year} [Court case]{.layer-badge}

No. The power to recognize foreign states and governments belongs to the President alone, and Sec. 214(d) of the Foreign Relations Authorization Act, Fiscal Year 2003, which required the listing, unconstitutionally infringed it.

[Read it: [opinion](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-576/pdf/USREPORTS-576-1.pdf)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="zivotofsky-2015"> I have read this</label>
:::

## Further reading

- [Title 10 U.S.C.](../../statutes/title10-usc.qmd){.subj}: The title of the U.S. Code that governs the armed forces: their organization, command, personnel, training, procurement, and reserve components.
- [Title 50 U.S.C.](../../statutes/title50-usc.qmd){.subj}: The title of the U.S. Code that collects the laws on war powers, emergency powers, intelligence, and economic defense.
- [Title 22 U.S.C.](../../statutes/title22-usc.qmd){.subj}: The title of the U.S. Code for diplomacy and foreign assistance. It holds the State Department's authorities, the Foreign Service, foreign aid, arms export controls, and most country-specific sanctions and policy statutes.
- [Title 32 U.S.C.](../../statutes/title32-usc.qmd){.subj}: The title of the U.S. Code for the National Guard when it is not in federal service. It governs organization, federal funding, and training of the Guard while it remains under the command of state governors.

## Key terms

**Positive law title**
:   A U.S. Code title Congress has itself enacted, so the Code text is the law. Titles 10 and 32 are positive law; Titles 22 and 50 are not, so for them the Statutes at Large control.

**Statutes at Large**
:   The official chronological publication of every law as enacted, cited by volume and page, for example 87 Stat. 555.

**Declaration of war**
:   A joint resolution or act under Article I declaring that a state of war exists. Congress has passed eleven, in five wars, the last in 1942.

## Issues for Congress

Questions that recur in oversight and legislation, with the main arguments on each side. There is no answer key; they are for discussion and briefing preparation.

### 1. Should Congress return to formal declarations of war, or keep relying on authorizations for use of force?

Congress has not declared war since 1942 ([Declarations of War](../../statutes/declarations-of-war.qmd)); statutory authorizations now do that work.

- Proponents of declarations argue they force a clear, accountable decision and carry legal consequences, such as triggering the [Alien Enemies Act](../../statutes/alien-enemies-1798.qmd), that authorizations do not.
- Others argue declarations fit wars between states, not operations against non-state groups, and that tailored authorizations can set purpose, scope, and duration more precisely.

### 2. How much deference should Congress give the executive in foreign affairs?

[Curtiss-Wright](../../cases/curtiss-wright-1936.qmd) and [Zivotofsky v. Kerry](../../cases/zivotofsky-2015.qmd) point in different directions on the reach of the President's foreign affairs power.

- Those favoring deference cite the need for speed, secrecy, and a single voice abroad, and the President's recognition and diplomatic powers.
- Those favoring a stronger congressional role cite Congress's Article I powers over war, commerce, and money, and [Justice Jackson's point](../../cases/youngstown-1952.qmd) that presidential power is weakest when it runs against Congress.

## Check yourself

Try to answer each question before opening it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 1. Which branch holds the power to declare war, and which commands the forces once committed?

Congress declares war, raises and supports armies, provides a navy, and makes rules for the forces under Article I, Section 8; the President is commander in chief under Article II. The [Constitution (war powers)](../../statutes/constitution-war-powers.qmd) page lays out the clauses and the undefined ground between them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 2. How many declarations of war has Congress passed, and in which conflicts?

Eleven, in five conflicts, from the War of 1812 through the Second World War. See [Declarations of War](../../statutes/declarations-of-war.qmd). Later conflicts were fought under statutory authorizations instead.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 3. Which of the Alien and Sedition Acts is still in force, and what triggers it?

The [Alien Enemies Act](../../statutes/alien-enemies-1798.qmd). It applies during a declared war or an invasion or predatory incursion by a foreign nation or government, and lets the President detain, restrict, and remove nationals of the hostile country.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 4. Why does it matter whether a U.S. Code title is positive law?

In a positive law title, such as [Title 10](../../statutes/title10-usc.qmd), the Code text is the law itself. In a non-positive title such as [Title 50](../../statutes/title50-usc.qmd), the Code is only evidence of the law, and the enacted text in the Statutes at Large controls if they differ.
:::
